idiom_name: right-biased Either[Error, A] composed in for-comprehensions
implementation_notes: Scala's standard library already carries the contract: Either[+A, +B] with the convention Left = failure and Right = success, right-biased map/flatMap so a for-comprehension chains fallible steps and stops at the first Left exactly like a railway, with the failure track keeping its value. Try[T] is the sibling form that captures exceptions at the boundary (Success/Failure), and Either is the type to prefer once the failure is a domain value. Nothing needs hand-writing: the composition syntax is the language's, and a match on Left/Right is the terminal handler. for-comprehensions over Either do not support guards or refutable patterns, so filtered steps convert to Option or use an explicit helper.
pitfalls: Left values often need an explicit type argument or inference produces Either[Double, Nothing]; annotate the error type once in the method signature.
for-comprehensions over Either have no withFilter, so guards and refutable patterns are compile errors - convert to Option or destructure in two steps.
Mixing Try and Either in one chain needs explicit conversion (toEither/toTry), otherwise the types stop lining up.

variants.name: cats Validated (error accumulation)
variants.implementation_notes: The default Either chain fails fast; where the caller must see every problem, cats provides Validated[E, A] - Valid(a)/Invalid(e) - whose Applicative instance accumulates errors instead of short-circuiting, usually as ValidatedNel[E, A] collecting into a NonEmptyList through the |+| operator or mapN. The docs motivate it exactly with a signup form whose field errors should be reported together. Use it at accumulation points (form validation, configuration checking) and convert (toEither/andThen) where a step depends on a previous success; Either stays the general-purpose track, since Validated has no flatMap for dependent steps.
pitfalls: Validated accumulates only through its Applicative (mapN/|+|); it deliberately has no flatMap, so dependent steps must convert to Either first.
Mixing Either and Validated in one chain needs explicit conversions (toValidated/toEither); forgetting them surfaces as an implicit-resolution error rather than a type mismatch.
